But manned space activity by governments is probably winding down in the long-term. China is a bit behind the curve in thinking that these geopolitical merit badges and displays of national techno-industrial prowess still matter to anyone. The long-term theme of space activity for all the countries involved is living with slowly shrinking budgets and struggling to do more with less. And that can end only one way; the obsolescence of the astronaut by machines. No matter what sort of fanciful spacecraft we might imagine in the future, it can't compete in cost with digital minds that can travel space by telecommunications. So, ultimately, neither government or business need human beings out there to do any of the things they might want to do --except in the minor industry of tourism.

But in this seemingly depressing situation I see a great overlooked opportunity. There is an imminent entrepreneurial boom in space because the technologies that may be obsolescing the astronaut are also lowering the bar of access to space. We've always had CATS, but not in the form that suited our traditional space adventure fantasies. The advancing technologies of telerobotics, AI, ISRU, and in-space manufacturing mean a progressive reduction in the cost of access to space because launch costs are driven primarily by payload values. The more these technologies lower the value of payloads, the cheaper it gets to get into space. So while the future may not look so go for the traditional astronaut, things are actually looking better for the space settler who can now leverage these technologies on independent space development. But it won't be governments and corporations doing space settlement --they don't really have any use for that. It will be intentional communities that go to space to realise some novel model of The Good Life out there.
